title: Partition List
description: Brute force to optimized: extracting into two arrays versus an in-place stable two-chain partition technique.

blocks.text: Given the head of a linked list and a value x, partition it such that all nodes LESS THAN x come before all nodes GREATER THAN OR EQUAL to x. Preserve the original relative order of the nodes within each of the two partitions.

blocks.caption: Two chains are grown simultaneously (less-than-x and greater-or-equal-x), then joined together

blocks.text: Every node with a value strictly less than x should end up before every node with a value greater than or equal to x, while each group internally keeps its ORIGINAL relative order (this is a "stable" partition).

blocks.title: Analogy: Sorting Students Into Two Lines Without Reshuffling Either Line
blocks.text: Given a line of students each holding a number, and a threshold x, split them into a "below threshold" line and an "at-or-above threshold" line, walking through the original line once and sending each student to their appropriate new line as they are reached. Since students are always added to the END of their new line, each new line naturally preserves the order the students appeared in originally. Finally, the "at-or-above" line is placed directly after the "below" line.

blocks.caption: Two chains (less-than-x and greater-or-equal-x) grow simultaneously; the less chain's tail is finally linked to the geq chain's head

blocks.text: Before extracting values into arrays and rebuilding, notice that two separate chains (less-than-x and greater-or-equal-x) can be grown simultaneously in a single pass, simply by appending each node to whichever chain it belongs to.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Maintaining a separate "tail" pointer for each of the two target chains lets any node be appended to the correct chain in O(1) time, the moment it is examined.

Observation 2: Since nodes are always appended to the END of their chain (never inserted in the middle), each chain automatically preserves the original relative order of its members: this is exactly the "stable partition" property required.

Observation 3: Using a dummy head for EACH of the two chains avoids needing special-case logic for "is this the first node added to this chain."

Observation 4: After the single pass completes, the geq chain's tail must have its next pointer explicitly set to null, since it may still be pointing at whatever came after it in the ORIGINAL list (a stale pointer).

Observation 5: The final step is simply linking the less chain's tail directly to the geq chain's (dummy-skipped) head, joining the two chains into the final result.
This is a stable single-pass partition technique: two chains are grown independently using their own dummy heads and tail pointers, then joined at the very end.
Extract all values into two separate arrays based on their comparison to x, then concatenate the less-than array followed by the greater-or-equal array.

items: Walk through the list once, appending each value to a "less" array (if strictly less than x) or a "geq" array (if greater than or equal to x).
Concatenate the less array followed by the geq array to produce the final partitioned result.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Two separate arrays, filled via a single linear scan, naturally preserve each group's original relative order, since elements are appended in the order they are encountered.
Concatenating "less" before "geq" directly matches the required output structure.

blocks.text: Correctly partitions all values while preserving relative order within each group, since a single left-to-right scan naturally does this.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass to classify plus one to rebuild.
Space: O(n), for the two intermediate arrays.
Limitation: extracting into arrays ignores that the EXISTING nodes can simply be re-linked in place into two chains, then joined, achieving the same result in O(1) extra space.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force rebuilds two entirely new arrays. Instead, maintain two separate dummy-headed chains (less and geq) with their own tail pointers. Walk the original list once, appending each node directly to whichever chain's tail it belongs after. Finally, terminate the geq chain properly (its tail may still point at a stale "next"), and join the less chain's tail to the geq chain's head.

Initialize lessDummy and geqDummy, with lessTail and geqTail both starting at their respective dummies. Walk node through the original list: append it to the less chain if its value is < x, otherwise to the geq chain, always updating the corresponding tail. After the pass, set geqTail.next = null (cleanup), then lessTail.next = geqDummy.next (the join).
Grow the less-than-x and greater-or-equal-x chains simultaneously in a single pass, then join them.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: After the pass, geqTail.next is set to null, and lessTail.next is set to the geq chain's head, giving [1,2,2,4,3,5], matching the expected result.

codes.python:
def partition(head, x):
    less_dummy = ListNode(0)
    geq_dummy = ListNode(0)
    less_tail = less_dummy
    geq_tail = geq_dummy

    node = head
    while node:
        if node.val < x:
            less_tail.next = node                                          # append this node to the "less than x" chain
            less_tail = node
        else:
            geq_tail.next = node                                           # append this node to the "greater-or-equal x" chain
            geq_tail = node
        node = node.next

    geq_tail.next = None                                                   # terminate the geq chain (it may hold a stale next pointer)
    less_tail.next = geq_dummy.next                                        # join: less chain's tail connects to geq chain's head
    return less_dummy.next


if __name__ == "__main__":
    head = ListNode(1, ListNode(4, ListNode(3, ListNode(2, ListNode(5, ListNode(2))))))
    result = partition(head, 3)
    values = []
    while result:
        values.append(result.val)
        result = result.next
    print(values)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass through the list.
Space: O(1) extra, reusing the existing nodes.

Since each node is appended directly to the END of whichever chain it belongs to (never inserted elsewhere), both chains automatically preserve the original relative order of their members. The final geqTail.next = null step is essential because geqTail might still hold a "next" pointer left over from the ORIGINAL list (pointing at a node that has since been reassigned into the less chain), which would silently create an incorrect structure (or even a cycle) if left unset.

items: Two separate dummy nodes cleanly avoid any special-casing for "is this the first node in this chain," since lessTail and geqTail simply start there.
The explicit geqTail.next = null step is a subtle but essential correctness fix, addressing a stale pointer that would otherwise persist from the original list structure.
The single final join (lessTail.next = geqDummy.next) correctly handles even the case where one of the two chains ends up completely empty.

blocks.text: A stable partition of a linked list (splitting by a comparison, while preserving relative order) can be done in a single pass by growing two separate chains, each with its own tail pointer, then joining them at the end.

items: Forgetting to set geqTail.next = null after the pass, leaving a stale pointer from the original list structure that can corrupt the result or create a cycle.
Using a single dummy/tail pair and trying to insert into the middle of a growing list, which would not naturally preserve relative order the way appending to two separate tails does.
Mishandling the case where one partition ends up completely empty (for example, if every value is >= x).

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["Empty list","Both chains stay empty; the result is an empty list"],["Every value is less than x","The geq chain stays empty; the result is the list unchanged (in original order)"],["Every value is greater than or equal to x","The less chain stays empty; the result is the list unchanged (in original order)"]]}

items: Explicitly stating the "stable partition" requirement (preserving relative order within each group) up front shows awareness of exactly why a naive swap-based partition (like quicksort's in-place partition) would NOT work here.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Partition while PRESERVING RELATIVE ORDER" points toward growing two separate chains with their own tails (a stable partition), rather than an in-place swap-based partition.

items: Why can't a simple swap-based (quicksort-style) partition be used here? Swapping values in place would NOT preserve each group's original relative order, violating the stability requirement.

How would you extend this to partition into THREE groups (less than, equal to, greater than x)? A third dummy-headed chain (for values exactly equal to x) could be grown simultaneously, then all three joined in order.

How would you verify the geqTail.next = null step is actually necessary? Trace an example where geqTail's original "next" pointer (before reassignment) would otherwise still reference a node that has since moved into the less chain.
A "simultaneous multi-chain" technique shared conceptually with Odd Even Linked List elsewhere in this category, both growing two separate chains in a single pass before joining them.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (simultaneous two-chain partition): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Stable single-pass two-chain partition

Core Idea: Grow a "less than x" chain and a "greater-or-equal x" chain simultaneously, each with its own dummy head and tail pointer, preserving relative order by always appending to the tail, then join the two chains
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: The geq chain's tail must have its next pointer explicitly nulled after the pass, since it may still hold a stale reference from the original list
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Two dummy-headed chains, append by comparison to x, null the geq tail, then join less.tail to geq.head
